items.t: Type 2 diabetes not controlled by diet and exercise, in adults and children aged 10 years and over: alone when metformin is not tolerated, or added to other diabetes medicines.

src.q: Empagliflozin is indicated in adults and children aged 10 years and above for the treatment of insufficiently controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus as an adjunct to diet and exercise
as monotherapy when metformin is considered inappropriate due to intolerance

items.t: Symptomatic chronic heart failure (adults).

src.q: Empagliflozin is indicated in adults for the treatment of symptomatic chronic heart failure.

items.t: Chronic kidney disease (adults).

src.q: Empagliflozin is indicated in adults for the treatment of chronic kidney disease.

items.t: Should not be used in type 1 diabetes (ketoacidosis was more common in type 1 trials).

src.q: Empagliflozin should not be used in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus
Data from a clinical trial program in patients with type 1 diabetes showed increased ketoacidosis occurrence with common frequency

items.t: Start 10 mg once daily (alone or add-on). If tolerated, eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m² and tighter control is needed, increase to 25 mg once daily. Maximum 25 mg daily.

src.q: The recommended starting dose is 10 mg empagliflozin once daily for monotherapy and add-on combination therapy with other medicinal products for the treatment of diabetes.

In patients tolerating empagliflozin 10 mg once daily who have an eGFR ≥60 ml/min/1.73 m2 and need tighter glycaemic control, the dose can be increased to 25 mg once daily. The maximum daily dose is 25 mg

items.t: 10 mg once daily.

src.q: Heart failure The recommended dose is 10 mg empagliflozin once daily.

items.t: 10 mg once daily.

src.q: Chronic kidney disease The recommended dose is 10 mg empagliflozin once daily.

items.t: With a sulfonylurea or insulin: consider a lower dose of these to reduce hypoglycaemia risk.
items.tag: All indications, with sulfonylurea or insulin

src.q: When empagliflozin is used in combination with a sulphonylurea or with insulin, a lower dose of the sulphonylurea or insulin may be considered to reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia

items.t: Missed dose: take when remembered, but not a double dose on the same day.

src.q: If a dose is missed, it should be taken as soon as the patient remembers; however, a double dose should not be taken on the same day.

items.t: Elderly: no dose change for age; at 75 years and over consider the higher risk of volume depletion.

src.q: No dose adjustment is recommended based on age. In patients 75 years and older, an increased risk for volume depletion should be taken into account

items.t: Type 2 diabetes, children aged 10 years and over: start 10 mg once daily; if tolerated and more control is needed, increase to 25 mg once daily. No data in children with eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m² or under 10 years.

src.q: Paediatric population The recommended starting dose is 10 mg empagliflozin once daily.
No data are available for children with eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m² and children below 10 years of age.

items.t: Heart failure and chronic kidney disease: not established under 18 years.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of empagliflozin for the treatment of heart failure or for the treatment of chronic kidney disease in children under 18 years of age have not been established.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to empagliflozin or any excipient.

src.q: 4.3 Contraindications Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Ketoacidosis (rare, can be fatal; may occur with glucose below 14 mmol/L, and has occurred in people without diabetes). Assess at once if non-specific symptoms (nausea, vomiting, anorexia, abdominal pain, excessive thirst, difficulty breathing, confusion, unusual fatigue or sleepiness), whatever the glucose. Stop immediately if suspected or diagnosed.

src.q: Cases of ketoacidosis, including life-threatening and fatal cases, have been reported in patients with diabetes mellitus treated with SGLT2 inhibitors, including empagliflozin.
Although ketoacidosis is less likely to occur in patients without diabetes mellitus, cases have also been reported in these patients.
In patients where ketoacidosis is suspected or diagnosed, treatment with empagliflozin should be discontinued immediately.

items.t: Interrupt when hospitalised for major surgery or acute serious illness; monitor ketones (blood preferred). Restart when ketones are normal and the patient is stable.

src.q: Treatment should be interrupted in patients who are hospitalised for major surgical procedures or acute serious medical illnesses. Monitoring of ketones is recommended in these patients.
Treatment with empagliflozin may be restarted when the ketone values are normal and the patient's condition has stabilised.

items.t: Higher ketoacidosis risk (use with caution): low beta-cell reserve (low C-peptide, LADA, history of pancreatitis), restricted food intake or severe dehydration, reduced insulin doses, higher insulin needs from acute illness, surgery or alcohol abuse. Restarting after ketoacidosis on an SGLT2 inhibitor is not recommended unless another clear cause was found and resolved.

src.q: Patients who may be at higher risk of ketoacidosis include patients with a low beta-cell function reserve
SGLT2 inhibitors should be used with caution in these patients.

Restarting SGLT2 inhibitor treatment in patients with previous ketoacidosis while on SGLT2 inhibitor treatment is not recommended, unless another clear precipitating factor is identified and resolved.

items.t: Volume depletion: caution in known cardiovascular disease, antihypertensive users with a history of hypotension, and age 75 and over. In illness with fluid loss monitor volume status and electrolytes; consider interrupting until fluid loss is corrected.

src.q: caution should be exercised in patients for whom an empagliflozin-induced drop in blood pressure could pose a risk, such as patients with known cardiovascular disease, patients on anti-hypertensive therapy with a history of hypotension or patients aged 75 years and older
Temporary interruption of treatment with empagliflozin should be considered until the fluid loss is corrected.

items.t: Complicated urinary tract infections (pyelonephritis, urosepsis) have been reported; consider temporary interruption.

src.q: Temporary interruption of empagliflozin should be considered in patients with complicated urinary tract infections.

items.t: Fournier's gangrene: rare but life-threatening. If suspected, stop and start urgent treatment (antibiotics, surgical debridement).

src.q: If Fournier's gangrene is suspected, empagliflozin should be discontinued and prompt treatment (including antibiotics and surgical debridement) should be instituted.

items.t: Renal function: check before starting, at least yearly, and before starting any medicine that may harm renal function.

src.q: Prior to empagliflozin initiation and periodically during treatment, i.e. at least yearly
Prior to initiation of any concomitant medicinal product that may have a negative impact on renal function.

items.t: Lower limb amputation (mainly toes) seen with another SGLT2 inhibitor; counsel on preventive foot care.

src.q: Like for all diabetic patients it is important to counsel patients on routine preventative foot-care.

items.t: Hepatic injury reported in trials (causal link not established). Raised haematocrit: monitor and investigate pronounced rises.

src.q: Cases of hepatic injury have been reported with empagliflozin in clinical trials. A causal relationship between empagliflozin and hepatic injury has not been established.
Patients with pronounced elevations in haematocrit should be monitored and investigated for underlying haematological disease.

items.t: Contains lactose: patients with hereditary galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take it. Urine glucose tests will be positive; 1,5-AG assay is unreliable.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicinal product.
patients taking empagliflozin will test positive for glucose in their urine.

items.t: Thiazide and loop diuretics: may add to the diuretic effect and increase the risk of dehydration and hypotension.

src.q: Empagliflozin may add to the diuretic effect of thiazide and loop diuretics and may increase the risk of dehydration and hypotension

items.t: Insulin and insulin secretagogues (e.g. sulfonylureas): a lower dose of these may be needed to reduce hypoglycaemia risk.

src.q: a lower dose of insulin or an insulin secretagogue may be required to reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia when used in combination with empagliflozin

items.t: Age 75 and over: pay special attention to fluid intake with medicines that may cause volume depletion (e.g. diuretics, ACE inhibitors).

src.q: special attention should be given to their volume intake in case of co-administered medicinal products which may lead to volume depletion (e.g. diuretics, ACE inhibitors)

items.t: UGT enzyme inducers (e.g. rifampicin, phenytoin; not in this tool's list): co-treatment not recommended (may reduce efficacy); if needed, monitor glycaemic control.

src.q: Co-treatment with known inducers of UGT enzymes is not recommended due to a potential risk of decreased efficacy.
If an inducer of these UGT enzymes must be co-administered, monitoring of glycaemic control to assess response to empagliflozin is appropriate.

items.t: Lithium (not in this tool's list): levels may fall; monitor lithium more often after starting or dose changes.

src.q: Empagliflozin may increase renal lithium excretion and the blood lithium levels may be decreased.
Serum concentration of lithium should be monitored more frequently after empagliflozin initiation and dose changes.

items.t: No clinically relevant interaction found with metformin, glimepiride, sitagliptin, linagliptin, warfarin, verapamil, simvastatin, hydrochlorothiazide, digoxin or oral contraceptives.

src.q: the pharmacokinetics of empagliflozin were not influenced by co-administration with metformin, glimepiride, pioglitazone, sitagliptin, linagliptin, warfarin, verapamil, ramipril, simvastatin, torasemide and hydrochlorothiazide.

empagliflozin had no clinically relevant effect on the pharmacokinetics of metformin, glimepiride, pioglitazone, sitagliptin, linagliptin, simvastatin, warfarin, ramipril, digoxin, diuretics and oral contraceptives.

items.t: eGFR < 20 mL/min/1.73 m²: starting treatment is not recommended (limited experience).

src.q: Due to limited experience, it is not recommended to initiate treatment with empagliflozin in patients with an eGFR <20 ml/min/1.73 m2.

items.t: eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m²: the daily dose is 10 mg.

src.q: In patients with an eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2 the daily dose of empagliflozin is 10 mg.

items.t: Type 2 diabetes: glucose-lowering effect reduced when eGFR < 45 and likely absent < 30 mL/min/1.73 m²; if eGFR falls below 45, consider additional glucose-lowering treatment if needed.

src.q: In patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus, the glucose lowering efficacy of empagliflozin is reduced in patients with an eGFR <45 ml/min/1.73 m2 and likely absent in patients with an eGFR <30 ml/min/1.73 m2.
if eGFR falls below 45 ml/min/1.73 m2, additional glucose lowering treatment should be considered if needed

items.t: No dose adjustment in hepatic impairment. Severe hepatic impairment: exposure increased and experience limited, so not recommended.

src.q: No dose adjustment is required for patients with hepatic impairment.
Therapeutic experience in patients with severe hepatic impairment is limited and therefore not recommended for use in this population

items.t: SmPC: no human data; animal studies showed effects on postnatal development. As a precaution, it is preferable to avoid in pregnancy.

src.q: However, animal studies have shown adverse effects on postnatal development
As a precautionary measure, it is preferable to avoid the use of empagliflozin during pregnancy.

items.t: BUMPS: treat type 2 diabetes in pregnancy with metformin, plus insulin if needed; SGLT2 inhibitors are avoided as a precaution. With an unplanned pregnancy, keep taking it until reviewed promptly.

src.q: Type 2 diabetes during pregnancy should be treated with metformin, as well as insulin if required. Other antidiabetic drugs should not be used.
you should carry on with the drug you are taking until your appointment, as uncontrolled diabetes is risky for you and your baby

items.t: SmPC: should not be used during breastfeeding (excreted in animal milk; infant risk cannot be excluded).

src.q: A risk to the newborns/infants cannot be excluded. Empagliflozin should not be used during breast-feeding.

items.t: SPS: insulin or metformin are the preferred choices; limited or no published information on other antidiabetic medicines.

src.q: Insulin or metformin are the preferred choices during breastfeeding.
limited or no published information on the use of other antidiabetic (blood-glucose lowering) medicines during breastfeeding.

items.t: No human fertility studies; animal studies show no harmful effect on fertility.

src.q: No studies on the effect on human fertility have been conducted for empagliflozin. Animal studies do not indicate direct or indirect harmful effects with respect to fertility

items.t: Hypoglycaemia when used with a sulfonylurea or insulin (the most frequent reaction in type 2 diabetes trials).

src.q: The most frequently reported adverse reaction was hypoglycaemia when used with sulphonylurea or insulin

items.t: Genital infections (vaginal thrush, vulvovaginitis, balanitis): about 4% vs 1% with placebo, more in women.

src.q: Vaginal moniliasis, vulvovaginitis, balanitis and other genital infections were reported more frequently in patients treated with empagliflozin (empagliflozin 10 mg: 4.0%, empagliflozin 25 mg: 3.9%) compared to placebo (1.0%).

items.t: Urinary tract infection (8.8% with 10 mg vs 7.2% placebo) and increased urination (about 3.5% vs 1.4%).

src.q: The overall frequency of urinary tract infection reported as adverse event was similar in patients treated with empagliflozin 25 mg and placebo (7.0% and 7.2%) and higher in empagliflozin 10 mg (8.8%).

Increased urination (including the predefined terms pollakiuria, polyuria, and nocturia) was observed at higher frequencies in patients treated with empagliflozin (empagliflozin 10 mg: 3.5%, empagliflozin 25 mg: 3.3%) compared to placebo (1.4%).

items.t: Volume depletion: the most frequent reaction in heart failure trials (11.4% vs 9.7%); more frequent at 75 years and over.

src.q: The most frequent adverse reaction of the pooled EMPEROR-Reduced and EMPEROR-Preserved studies was volume depletion (empagliflozin 10 mg: 11.4%. placebo: 9.7%).
The frequency of volume depletion events was increased in patients 75 years and older

items.t: Ketoacidosis (may occur with near-normal glucose): stop immediately and assess.

src.q: In patients where ketoacidosis is suspected or diagnosed, treatment with empagliflozin should be discontinued immediately.

items.t: Fournier's gangrene: seek care for genital or perineal pain, tenderness, redness or swelling with fever or malaise; stop and treat urgently.

src.q: Patients should be advised to seek medical attention if they experience a combination of symptoms of pain, tenderness, erythema, or swelling in the genital or perineal area, with fever or malaise.

if Fournier's gangrene is suspected, stop the SGLT2 inhibitor and urgently start treatment
